domain_title: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications

questions.scenario: An e-commerce company runs predictable, steady inference traffic on Claude 3 Sonnet at ~500,000 tokens/minute, 24x7, for 9 months out of the year. Throttling errors during peak hours are unacceptable.
questions.stem: Which Bedrock throughput model is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: On-Demand only — pay per token at standard rate.
options.why: At steady high volume, On-Demand totals more than committed pricing AND offers no capacity guarantee.
Steady high volume + capacity guarantee = Provisioned Throughput. 6-month commit gives the best per-token rate for a 9-month workload.
Batch is async, up to 24h SLA. Wrong for 24x7 interactive workload.
OpenSearch is a search engine, not an FM.

questions.knowledge_point: Provisioned Throughput (PT): 1- or 6-month commit, Model Units (MUs) guarantee capacity. Cost-effective for STEADY HIGH-VOLUME workloads. REQUIRED for hosting custom (fine-tuned) models.
questions.trap_alert: PT is overkill for bursty/sporadic traffic. Match commit length to workload duration.

questions.scenario: A pharma team must summarize 200,000 PubMed abstracts for an internal knowledge graph. The task can run overnight; per-summary latency does not matter.

options.text: Bedrock Batch Inference — submit a JSONL file to S3 and receive results in S3 at ~50% discount.
options.why: Batch is purpose-built for high-volume async jobs with substantial per-token discount.

options.text: Lambda fan-out calling On-Demand InvokeModel for each abstract.
options.why: Functional but pays full On-Demand rate AND adds Lambda invocation cost.
Overkill for a one-night job; commit duration mismatched to use.
KBs are for RAG retrieval; not for offline bulk processing of documents.

questions.knowledge_point: Bedrock Batch Inference: ~50% lower per-token cost, async, ≤24h SLA, S3 input/output JSONL. Right tool for offline bulk jobs.
questions.trap_alert: If the question says 'overnight' or 'latency not important' AND 'cost matters', Batch is almost always the answer.

questions.scenario: A coding assistant repeatedly includes the same 12,000-token system prompt with engineering standards and code-style examples on every Claude invocation. Hundreds of requests per minute.
questions.stem: Which Bedrock feature MOST reduces cost?

options.text: Bedrock Prompt Caching — mark the system prompt as a cache breakpoint.
options.why: Repeated long prefixes are exactly what prompt caching targets. After the WRITE, subsequent reads cost ~10% of the base input price.
Doesn't address the repeated input tokens cost; may reduce per-call output cost only.
PT changes capacity/commit, not per-token cost structure for repeated prefixes.

options.text: Compress the system prompt by half.
options.why: Helps marginally but caching offers much bigger savings for repeated content.

questions.knowledge_point: Bedrock Prompt Caching (on supported Claude models): cache control breakpoints on system/tools/messages. Cache WRITE ≈ 1.25× base, READ ≈ 0.1× base, 5-min TTL.
questions.trap_alert: Break-even is ~2–3 reuses of the cached prefix within 5 minutes. Don't cache one-shots.

questions.stem: Which statement about Amazon Bedrock prompt caching is TRUE?

options.text: Cached prefixes have a roughly 5-minute TTL; cache writes cost more than non-cached input; cache reads cost a fraction of the base input price.
options.why: Documented pricing: write ≈ 1.25× base, read ≈ 0.1× base, ~5 min TTL.
TTL is roughly 5 minutes, not 24h.
Cache writes incur a higher per-token cost than non-cached input.

options.text: Caching is automatic on all models.
options.why: Caching is opt-in (set cache_control breakpoints) and supported on specific models.

questions.knowledge_point: Prompt cache pricing/TTL: 5-min TTL; write ~1.25× base input; read ~0.1× base input. Need ~2–3 reuses to break even.
questions.trap_alert: Don't expect free writes or 24h TTL — quick to misremember.

questions.scenario: A team needs to classify support tickets into 10 categories. Volume is high; precision is acceptable in the mid-90s; cost matters more than depth of reasoning.
questions.stem: Which Bedrock model is MOST cost-effective for this workload?

options.why: Haiku is the cheapest/fastest in the Claude 3 family — ideal for high-volume classification where deep reasoning isn't required.
Most expensive — overkill for classification.
Image generation model.
Text-to-speech.

questions.knowledge_point: Match model tier to task complexity. Haiku/Nova Micro for high-volume light tasks; Sonnet/Nova Pro for balanced; Opus/Nova Premier for deep reasoning.
questions.trap_alert: Don't pick Opus by default. Opus's cost is multiple× of Haiku for marginal benefit on simple tasks.

questions.scenario: A new application hits 429 ThrottlingException errors on Bedrock during peak traffic. Workload cannot be moved to async.
questions.stem: Which is the MOST EFFECTIVE first step?

options.text: Request a Service Quotas increase for the model's TPM (tokens per minute) and RPM (requests per minute), and consider a cross-region inference profile for capacity overflow.
options.why: Throttling = quota wall. Raise the quota; cross-region inference can spread peak load. Both are documented levers.

options.text: Add exponential backoff and call it a day.
options.why: Helps for transient spikes but does not raise the actual ceiling.

options.text: Switch to Provisioned Throughput as the first move.
options.why: PT solves it but is a 1mo/6mo commit — heavier than necessary as first step.
Has no effect on Bedrock-side quotas.

questions.knowledge_point: Bedrock throttling levers: (1) request Service Quotas increase, (2) cross-region inference profile, (3) Provisioned Throughput for sustained high load, (4) exponential backoff to soak transient spikes.
questions.trap_alert: Backoff alone is not 'most effective'. Quota increase + cross-region is the documented combination.

questions.scenario: An ML team fine-tuned Claude 3 Haiku on customer-support transcripts. They want to serve the custom model on Bedrock for production inference.

options.text: Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the custom model — custom-model hosting requires PT.
options.why: Custom (fine-tuned) models on Bedrock require Provisioned Throughput to host. On-Demand is for foundation models only.
On-Demand does NOT support custom models. PT is required for hosting.
Batch is for async jobs and the underlying access still requires PT for the custom model.
Custom Model Import is for bringing external fine-tuned weights into Bedrock — orthogonal to PT requirement for hosting.

questions.knowledge_point: Hosting custom models on Bedrock = Provisioned Throughput required. Base FMs run On-Demand; custom (fine-tuned) ones require PT.
questions.trap_alert: If the question mentions 'fine-tuned' AND 'serve', think PT immediately.

questions.scenario: A chat UI has high p99 latency on Bedrock responses. The workload is interactive (one user at a time) and uses Claude 3 Sonnet.
questions.stem: Which change is LIKELY to reduce p99 latency the MOST?

options.text: Switch to InvokeModelWithResponseStream and a smaller-tier model (Haiku) where quality permits.
options.why: Streaming reduces perceived latency dramatically; smaller-tier model reduces true latency. Combo addresses both.
Cap is not the actual length; doesn't reduce latency.

options.text: Add CloudFront in front of Bedrock.
options.why: CloudFront cannot proxy Bedrock invocations as a cache.

options.text: Provision a larger Lambda memory size.
options.why: Marginal; Bedrock call latency dominates.

questions.knowledge_point: Latency levers for Bedrock: smaller model, streaming, regional proximity, prompt brevity, prompt caching, provisioned throughput (reduces queueing).
questions.trap_alert: max_tokens is a CAP, not the actual output length. Doesn't reduce latency by itself.

questions.scenario: A team in us-east-1 is hitting Claude 3.5 Sonnet capacity limits during business hours. Migrating to another region is not acceptable.
questions.stem: Which feature MOST helps without changing the home region?

options.text: Use a cross-region inference profile that allows Bedrock to route invocations to additional regions while keeping the home region as us-east-1.
options.why: Cross-region inference profiles let you scale capacity across regions transparently while keeping callers in one home region.
Question excludes home-region change.
Different model family; doesn't address Claude capacity.
Unrelated to capacity.

questions.knowledge_point: Cross-region inference profile = capacity + resilience by routing to multiple regions. Quotas tracked at the home region; data movement implications must be considered.
questions.trap_alert: Cross-region inference can violate data residency. Read the scenario carefully if EU/regulatory.

questions.scenario: A finance team wants automated alerts when Bedrock spend spikes unexpectedly versus historical patterns.
questions.stem: Which AWS service MOST DIRECTLY supports this?

options.text: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection scoped to the Amazon Bedrock service.
options.why: Cost Anomaly Detection uses ML to detect unexpected spend changes per service / linked account / tag. Native fit.

options.text: AWS Budgets with a fixed monthly threshold.
options.why: Useful but threshold-based, not anomaly-aware.
Cost-optimization recommendations, not anomaly detection on Bedrock.
Log queries, not cost analytics.

questions.knowledge_point: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection = ML-based anomaly alerts per service/account/tag. Use for Bedrock to catch unexpected spend changes.
questions.trap_alert: Budgets ≠ Anomaly Detection. Budgets are threshold rules; Cost Anomaly Detection is ML-based pattern monitoring.

questions.scenario: A SaaS product has a predictable baseline load 24x7 plus 4× spikes during product launches twice a year.
questions.stem: Which throughput strategy is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: Use Provisioned Throughput sized to the baseline, and let On-Demand absorb the launch spikes (hybrid).
options.why: Hybrid pattern: PT for the steady floor (cheap per token); On-Demand for the rare peaks. Avoids over-committing for occasional spikes.
Wastes capacity 99% of the year.
Pays full per-token cost on the steady high baseline — leaves savings on the table.
Batch is async; assume the workload is interactive.

questions.knowledge_point: Hybrid throughput pattern: PT for baseline (committed cheap rate) + On-Demand for bursts (no commit). Best of both for variable load.
questions.trap_alert: Don't provision for peak — that's the classic over-commit mistake. Provision for floor.

questions.scenario: A pricing experiment found that switching from Claude 3 Opus to Claude 3 Sonnet for a content generation pipeline reduced costs by ~80% with negligible quality drop.
questions.stem: Which principle does this MOST illustrate?

options.text: Right-size the model: pick the smallest model in the family that meets quality requirements.
options.why: Model right-sizing is the highest-ROI single lever for GenAI cost optimization.

options.text: Always use the largest available model.
options.why: Opposite principle — usually wasteful.

options.text: Prompt brevity is always more impactful than model choice.
options.why: Brevity helps but model tier change generally has a larger absolute impact.
Only when utilization justifies the commit.

questions.knowledge_point: Cost optimization first move: right-size the MODEL. Then prompt brevity, caching, batch, PT — in roughly that order of expected ROI.
questions.trap_alert: Don't reflexively pick Opus or Premier. The exam rewards model right-sizing.

questions.scenario: A team must receive an email when monthly Bedrock spend crosses $5,000.

options.text: AWS Budgets with a cost budget scoped to the Bedrock service and an SNS-email subscriber on the threshold.
options.why: Budgets are the threshold-alert primitive in AWS Billing — scope to Bedrock and notify via SNS.
Anomaly Detection is for unexpected pattern changes, not fixed thresholds.
Explorer is for analysis; no alerting.
Advisory checks; not threshold alerts.

questions.knowledge_point: Cost thresholds = AWS Budgets. Anomaly patterns = Cost Anomaly Detection. Analysis = Cost Explorer. Pick by intent.
questions.trap_alert: Threshold alert vs anomaly alert — different products. Read the verb in the scenario.

questions.stem: Which statements about Amazon Bedrock Batch Inference are TRUE? (Select TWO)

options.text: Input and output are JSONL files in Amazon S3.
options.why: Documented Batch I/O format and storage.

options.text: Per-token pricing is reduced by approximately 50% versus On-Demand.
options.why: Documented ~50% discount for batch.

options.text: Batch jobs complete in under 1 minute regardless of size.
options.why: Up to 24h SLA — not sub-minute.

options.text: Batch supports streaming responses to the caller.
options.why: Batch is asynchronous; results are written to S3, not streamed.
IAM still applies.

questions.knowledge_point: Batch Inference: ~50% discount, JSONL S3 in/out, up to 24h SLA, async only. IAM enforced as normal.
questions.trap_alert: If the scenario needs streaming or sub-minute responses, Batch is the WRONG answer regardless of cost benefit.

questions.scenario: A team builds an unpredictable, rarely-used internal tool that may sit idle for weeks and suddenly process a few prompts.
questions.stem: Which Bedrock throughput model is MOST appropriate?

options.why: Pay-per-use with no commitment is the right fit for sporadic, low-utilization workloads.
Paying for idle capacity for weeks — wasteful.
Async with up to 24h SLA — wrong if the tool is interactive.
Capacity routing, not a throughput model on its own.

questions.knowledge_point: Throughput-mode decision rule: sporadic/low → On-Demand; steady high → Provisioned; offline bulk → Batch.
questions.trap_alert: PT is overkill for sporadic workloads. The cheapest mode for idle-with-spikes is On-Demand.
